items.title: The President: Election, Term & Powers
items.body:
### The President of India

**In one line**
The President is India's head of state — the formal, ceremonial top of the Union executive — while real governing power lies with the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.

**Why it is asked**
Articles, the election method, veto types and emergency powers are factual favourites in APPSC/UPSC Prelims, and "nominal versus real executive" is a staple Mains theme.

**The story**
The Constitution (Art 52) creates the office of President as head of the Union. Article 53 vests the Union's executive power in the President, but Article 74 says the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers — advice the 42nd and 44th Amendments made binding (the President may return it once for reconsideration, then must accept it). So on paper the office is powerful; in practice the President is a constitutional head who normally signs where advised.

The President is **not** directly elected. An **electoral college** chooses the President by **proportional representation using the single transferable vote** and a secret ballot (Art 54-55). The term is five years (Art 56), re-election is allowed (Art 57), and the oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India.

**Who can become President (Art 58)?** A citizen of India who has **completed 35 years of age**, is **qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha**, and holds no office of profit. **Article 62** provides for filling a vacancy in the office: the election to fill a vacancy caused by the end of the term must be completed **before the term expires**, and a casual vacancy (death, resignation, removal) must be filled within six months.

**Picture it**

| Power | Article |
|---|---|
| Ordinance when Parliament is not in session | Art 123 |
| Assent to or veto a bill | Art 111 |
| Pardon — for punishment for an offence against a Union law, punishment by a court-martial (military court), and any sentence of death | Art 72 |
| Proclaim the three emergencies | Art 352 / 356 / 360 |

**Terms explained**
- **Electoral college** = the group that elects the President: elected members of both Houses of Parliament plus elected members of the State (and Delhi and Puducherry) Legislative Assemblies.
- **Single transferable vote** = each voter ranks candidates 1, 2, 3…; a winner needs a fixed quota of votes, and surplus or lowest votes are transferred by rank until someone reaches the quota.
- **Veto** = the power to refuse or delay a bill: absolute = withhold assent altogether; suspensive = return the bill (Parliament can override by re-passing it); pocket = neither assent, reject nor return the bill, keeping it pending indefinitely.

**Don't confuse**
- The President is elected by the single transferable vote, but a bill at a **joint sitting** is passed by a **simple majority** — different rules.
- The President has **no veto** over a Constitutional Amendment Bill (the 24th Amendment made assent compulsory) and no suspensive veto over a Money Bill.

**Remember it**
"Advised, not powerless" — the President must act on advice, yet keeps real discretion when no party clearly wins and when guarding the Constitution.

**TL;DR**
- President = head of state, nominal executive (Art 52-53); real power with the Council of Ministers (Art 74).
- Elected indirectly by an electoral college using the single transferable vote (Art 54-55); five-year term (Art 56).
- Key powers: ordinance (Art 123), assent/veto (Art 111), pardon (Art 72), emergencies (Art 352/356/360).
- Three veto types — absolute, suspensive, pocket; none over a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
keyPoints: President is elected indirectly by an electoral college using single transferable vote (Art 54-55).
Term of the President is 5 years (Art 56), with re-election permitted; oath administered by the CJI.
Article 123 gives the President ordinance-making power when Parliament is not in session.
Article 72 pardoning power uniquely covers death sentences and court-martial sentences, unlike a Governor's.
Three emergencies: National (Art 352), President's Rule (Art 356), Financial (Art 360).
Eligibility (Art 58): citizen, completed 35 years, qualified for Lok Sabha membership; Art 62 governs filling a vacancy.

items.title: Vice-President, PM & Council of Ministers
items.body:
### Vice-President, Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers

**In one line**
These three form the working core of the Union executive: the Vice-President presides over the Rajya Sabha, while the Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers that actually runs the government.

**Why it is asked**
Election and removal of the Vice-President, the six-month membership rule for ministers, and the 15% cap on the Council's size are common statement-based questions.

**The story**
The **Vice-President (Art 63-71)** is the second-highest constitutional office. By default (Art 64) the Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and acts as President for a maximum of six months if that office falls vacant. The Vice-President is elected by an electoral college consisting of the members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament, through the single transferable vote. Removal is unusual: the resolution can start **only in the Rajya Sabha** (needing an effective majority with 14 days' notice) and must then be agreed to by the Lok Sabha — there is no elaborate impeachment as there is for the President.

The **Prime Minister (Art 75)** is appointed by the President. The Constitution lays down no procedure, so convention governs: the President invites the leader who commands a Lok Sabha majority. A person not yet a member of either House can be made Prime Minister but must become a member within **six months**, or lose the post.

The **Council of Ministers (Art 74 and 75)** aids and advises the President. The 91st Amendment (2003) caps the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, at **15% of the Lok Sabha's strength**, and the Council is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha**. The smaller inner ring of senior ministers is the Cabinet, which meets often and takes the binding policy decisions.

**Picture it**

| Body | Core rule |
|---|---|
| Vice-President | Ex-officio Rajya Sabha Chairman (Art 64); removal starts in Rajya Sabha |
| Prime Minister | Appointed by President (Art 75); a non-member gets six months |
| Council of Ministers | ≤ 15% of Lok Sabha (91st Amendment); collective responsibility |
| Cabinet | Inner body of senior ministers; meets weekly |

**Terms explained**
- **Ex-officio** = holding one post automatically because of another (the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha simply by being Vice-President).
- **Collective responsibility** = the whole Council stands or falls together; if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, every minister resigns, even those from the Rajya Sabha.
- **Effective majority** = a majority of the members then in office (vacancies not counted).

**Don't confuse**
- The Vice-President's removal starts **only in the Rajya Sabha**; a no-confidence motion against the government lies **only in the Lok Sabha**.
- The **Council of Ministers** is the wide body; the **Cabinet** is its small core — not the other way round.

**Remember it**
"VP chairs the Upper House; the PM survives on the Lower House" — the Rajya Sabha has the Vice-President, but the government lives only on Lok Sabha confidence.

**TL;DR**
- Vice-President (Art 63-71): ex-officio Rajya Sabha Chairman; removal initiated only in the Rajya Sabha.
- PM (Art 75): appointed by the President; a non-member must enter Parliament within six months.
- Council of Ministers ≤ 15% of Lok Sabha strength (91st Amendment, 2003); collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
- Cabinet = the small inner core of the wider Council of Ministers.
keyPoints: The Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Art 64) and acts as President for max 6 months.
A Vice-President's removal resolution can be initiated only in the Rajya Sabha (Art 67).
The PM is appointed under Art 75; a non-member must enter Parliament within 6 months.
Council of Ministers is capped at 15% of Lok Sabha strength by the 91st CAA, 2003.
Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; the Cabinet is its smaller inner body.

items.title: Parliament: Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha
items.body:
### Parliament — Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha

**In one line**
Parliament is India's Union law-making body, with three parts — the President, the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People).

**Why it is asked**
The two Houses' strength, term and exclusive powers are among the most frequently tested polity facts.

**The story**
Parliament consists of the **President, the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha**. **Articles 79 to 122 in Part V** deal with its organisation and powers. It is modelled on the **British Westminster system** rather than the American (presidential) system. The President, though not a member of either House, is counted as part of Parliament because the President summons, prorogues and dissolves the Houses and gives assent to bills.

The **Lok Sabha** is the directly elected House: voters choose members by universal adult suffrage on a first-past-the-post basis. It is the House of confidence — only it can remove the government and only it can start a Money Bill. The **Rajya Sabha** is indirectly elected by the State Legislative Assemblies (plus 12 members nominated by the President) and is a **permanent House**: it is never dissolved, and one-third of its members retire every two years, giving continuity.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Rajya Sabha | Lok Sabha |
|---|---|---|
| Article | 80 | 81 |
| Maximum strength | 250 (238 elected + 12 nominated) | 552 |
| Current strength | 245 | 543 |
| How elected | Indirect (Assemblies), STV | Direct, first-past-the-post |
| Term | Permanent; 1/3 retire every 2 years | 5 years (Art 83) |
| Minimum age | 30 | 25 |
| Presiding officer | Chairman (Vice-President) | Speaker |

**The Speaker's key powers**
- Decides whether a bill is a **Money Bill**, and the decision is **final**.
- Decides questions of **disqualification under the Tenth Schedule** (anti-defection law); since Kihoto Hollohan (1992) this decision is open to judicial review.
- Presides over a **joint sitting** of both Houses.
- Does **NOT vote in the first instance**; the Speaker exercises only a **casting vote** when there is a tie.

**Terms explained**
- **First-past-the-post** = the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority.
- **Permanent House** = a House that is not dissolved as a whole; members leave in staggered batches, so the House always exists.
- **STV (single transferable vote)** = the ranked-ballot method used to elect Rajya Sabha members.

**Don't confuse**
- The **maximum** Lok Sabha strength is 552 (530 states + 20 UTs + 2 Anglo-Indians); the 104th Amendment (2019) ended the Anglo-Indian seats, so the effective maximum is now 550 and the present elected strength is 543.
- Only the **Lok Sabha** passes a no-confidence motion and starts Money Bills; only the **Rajya Sabha** can use Art 249 and Art 312.

**Remember it**
"Rajya Sabha = States plus permanence; Lok Sabha = people plus the power of the purse."

**TL;DR**
- Parliament (Art 79-122) = President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha, on the British model.
- Lok Sabha: directly elected, maximum 552 (now effectively 550), five-year term; Rajya Sabha: indirectly elected, maximum 250, permanent.
- The 104th Amendment (2019) ended the nomination of Anglo-Indian members.
- Lok Sabha only: no-confidence and Money Bills; Rajya Sabha only: Art 249 (State List law) and Art 312 (All India Services).
keyPoints: Parliament (Art 79-122) = President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha, on the British model.
Lok Sabha max strength 552, term 5 years; Rajya Sabha max 250, permanent with 1/3 retiring every 2 years.
104th Amendment (2019) abolished the nomination of Anglo-Indian members.
Only the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion and originates Money Bills.
Rajya Sabha's exclusive powers: Art 249 (State List law) and Art 312 (All India Services).
Speaker: certifies Money Bills (final), decides Tenth Schedule disqualification, presides at joint sittings, and has only a casting vote (no first-instance vote).

items.title: Bills, Money Bills & Joint Sittings
items.body:
### Bills, Money Bills and Joint Sittings

**In one line**
A bill is a draft law; how it travels through Parliament depends on its type — ordinary, money, financial, or constitutional amendment.

**Why it is asked**
Money Bill rules (where it starts, the 14-day limit, the Speaker's final word) and the short list of joint sittings are classic Prelims traps.

**The story**
An **ordinary bill** can start in either House, and both Houses have equal power over it. A **Money Bill (Art 110)** is special: it deals only with taxes, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund, can be introduced **only in the Lok Sabha** on the President's recommendation, and the Rajya Sabha may merely recommend changes. If the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within **14 days**, it is deemed passed. The **Speaker certifies** whether a bill is a Money Bill, and that decision is final. A **Constitutional Amendment Bill (Art 368)** needs a special majority in each House and cannot go to a joint sitting.

When the two Houses disagree on an **ordinary** bill, the President may summon a **joint sitting (Art 108)**, presided over by the Speaker, where the bill passes by a majority of members present and voting. Because the Lok Sabha is larger, it usually prevails.

**Picture it**

| Bill | Where it starts | Rajya Sabha's role |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary | Either House | Equal power to amend or reject |
| Money (Art 110) | Lok Sabha only | Recommend only; return within 14 days |
| Financial | Either House | Amend or reject (like ordinary) |
| Constitutional Amendment (Art 368) | Either House | Must pass by special majority |

**Terms explained**
- **Consolidated Fund** = the government's main account, into which all revenues flow and from which spending is drawn.
- **Special majority (Art 368)** = a majority of the total membership of a House and at least two-thirds of the members present and voting.
- **Joint sitting** = a combined meeting of both Houses to break a deadlock over an ordinary bill.

**Don't confuse**
- A joint sitting can be called for an **ordinary** bill only — **never** for a Money Bill or a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
- The Speaker **certifies** a Money Bill and **presides** at a joint sitting — two separate powers.

**Remember it**
Only three joint sittings have ever happened — **Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978) and POTA (2002)**: "Dowry, Banking, POTA".

**TL;DR**
- Money Bills (Art 110) start only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha only recommends, within 14 days.
- The Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is final.
- Constitutional Amendment Bills need a special majority (Art 368) and are barred from joint sittings.
- Joint sitting (Art 108): Speaker presides; only three ever held — 1961, 1978, 2002.
keyPoints: Money Bills (Art 110) originate only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days.
The Speaker's certification of a Money Bill is final.
Constitutional Amendment Bills need a special majority in each House (Art 368).
Joint sitting (Art 108) is presided over by the Speaker and excludes Money and Amendment Bills.
Only three joint sittings: Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978), POTA (2002).

items.title: Sessions, Dissolution & Parliamentary Devices
items.body:
### Sessions, Dissolution and Parliamentary Devices

**In one line**
This topic covers how Parliament meets and breaks up (sessions, prorogation, dissolution) and the tools members use to raise issues and hold the government to account.

**Why it is asked**
The six-month gap rule, the adjournment-prorogation-dissolution ladder, which bills lapse, and Zero Hour versus Question Hour are recurring one-mark questions.

**The story**
The President summons each House on the Cabinet's advice, and the gap between two sessions must not exceed **six months** (Art 85). By convention there are three sessions a year — Budget, Monsoon and Winter.

Three terms describe how sittings end. **Adjournment** is a short break within a session, ordered by the presiding officer. **Prorogation** ends a whole session and is ordered by the President. **Dissolution** ends the very life of the Lok Sabha, after which fresh elections are held; the Rajya Sabha, being permanent, is never dissolved. When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, most bills tied to it lapse — but a bill already passed by both Houses and awaiting only the President's assent does **not** lapse.

Members raise matters through **devices**: **Question Hour** (the first hour of a sitting, with starred questions answered orally and unstarred ones in writing) and **Zero Hour** (an Indian innovation since 1962, not written in the rules, that follows Question Hour for urgent matters without notice).

**Picture it**

| Device | Effect | Who orders it |
|---|---|---|
| Adjournment | Short suspension of a sitting | Presiding officer |
| Prorogation | Ends a session | President |
| Dissolution | Ends the Lok Sabha's life | President (on Cabinet advice) |

**Terms explained**
- **Prorogation** = formally closing a session; pending business survives, but the House is not sitting.
- **Lapse** = a bill dies and must be introduced afresh in the new House.
- **No-confidence motion** = a motion that, if passed by the Lok Sabha, forces the entire Council of Ministers to resign; a **censure motion** can target one minister, must state reasons, and need not cause resignation.

**Don't confuse**
- **Adjournment** pauses a sitting; **prorogation** ends a session; **dissolution** ends the House — increasing order of finality.
- **Zero Hour** is not in the rules; **Question Hour** and the **Calling Attention Motion (1954)** are.

**Remember it**
"Adjourn, then prorogue, then dissolve" — a pause, then the end of the session, then the end of the House.

**TL;DR**
- Art 85: no more than six months between two sessions; three sessions by convention.
- Adjournment (presiding officer), then prorogation (ends session), then dissolution (ends Lok Sabha).
- A bill passed by both Houses and awaiting assent does not lapse on dissolution.
- Zero Hour = Indian innovation (1962), not in the rules; Question Hour is the first hour.
keyPoints: Article 85 mandates a gap of no more than six months between two parliamentary sessions.
Adjournment (presiding officer) vs prorogation (ends session) vs dissolution (ends Lok Sabha's life).
A bill passed by both Houses and awaiting the President's assent does not lapse on dissolution.
Zero Hour is an Indian innovation (since 1962), not mentioned in the rules; Question Hour is the first hour.
A No-Confidence Motion is directed at the whole Council of Ministers; a Censure Motion may target one minister and must state reasons.

items.title: Parliamentary Committees & the Union Budget
items.body:
### Parliamentary Committees and the Union Budget

**In one line**
Because the full House has little time, small committees do the detailed scrutiny of spending and policy, and the Budget is Parliament's yearly approval of the government's income and expenditure.

**Why it is asked**
The composition of the three financial committees and the Budget stages and cut motions are high-frequency facts.

**The story**
Parliament cannot examine every rupee on the floor, so **financial committees** act as its detailed auditors. The **Public Accounts Committee** checks the Comptroller and Auditor General's reports after money has been spent (a "post-mortem" body). The **Estimates Committee** suggests economies in planned spending. The **Committee on Public Undertakings** reviews public-sector enterprises. Alongside these, 24 **Departmental Standing Committees** (set up in 1993) examine each ministry's Demands for Grants and its bills. All their recommendations are advisory.

No demand for a grant can be made except on the recommendation of the President (**Art 113**). The **Budget** (the Annual Financial Statement, presented under Art 112) moves through six stages: presentation, general discussion, committee scrutiny, voting on Demands for Grants (only the Lok Sabha votes), passing the **Appropriation Bill** (which authorises drawing money from the Consolidated Fund) and finally the **Finance Bill** (which enacts the year's taxes).

**Picture it**

| Committee | Composition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Public Accounts Committee | 22 (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha) | Examines CAG reports; set up 1921 |
| Estimates Committee | 30 (Lok Sabha only) | Suggests economies; set up 1950 |
| Committee on Public Undertakings | 22 (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha) | Reviews public enterprises; set up 1964 |

**Terms explained**
- **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** = the constitutional auditor of all government accounts.
- **Demands for Grants** = the ministry-by-ministry spending requests the Lok Sabha votes on.
- **Cut motion** = a motion to reduce a demand: a **Policy Cut** reduces it to ₹1, an **Economy Cut** reduces it by a stated sum, and a **Token Cut** reduces it by ₹100.
- **Guillotine** = the Speaker putting all undiscussed demands to a single vote when time runs out.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Estimates Committee** (30 members) is the largest and has **only Lok Sabha** members; the **PAC** has 22 members drawn from both Houses.
- The **Appropriation Bill** lets money be withdrawn; the **Finance Bill** levies the taxes — two different bills.

**Remember it**
"PAC looks back, Estimates looks ahead" — the PAC audits money already spent, the Estimates Committee trims money about to be spent.

**TL;DR**
- PAC: 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS), examines CAG reports; Estimates: 30 LS members only; PUC: 22 members.
- 24 Departmental Standing Committees (since 1993); all recommendations are advisory.
- Budget = Annual Financial Statement (Art 112), six stages; only the Lok Sabha votes Demands for Grants.
- Cut motions: Policy (to ₹1), Economy (stated sum), Token (₹100); the Guillotine clears undiscussed demands.
keyPoints: PAC has 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS) and examines CAG reports; the Estimates Committee has 30 Lok Sabha members only.
24 Departmental Standing Committees (since 1993) scrutinise ministries; their recommendations are advisory.
The Budget is the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112 and passes through six parliamentary stages.
Only the Lok Sabha votes on Demands for Grants; charged expenditure is non-votable.
Cut motions: Policy Cut (to Re 1), Economy Cut (specified sum), Token Cut (₹100); the Guillotine votes undiscussed demands.

items.title: MPLADS, Administrative Reform & the Deputy Speaker
items.body:
### MPLADS, Administrative Reform and the Deputy Speaker

**In one line**
Three smaller but often-tested topics: the MP Local Area Development Scheme, the birth of India's personnel department, and the Lok Sabha's Deputy Speaker.

**Why it is asked**
These come from past-paper residual facts — the non-lapsable nature of MPLADS funds, the 1970 Department of Personnel, and the Deputy Speaker's election and removal.

**The story**
Under the **MPLAD Scheme**, every Member of Parliament recommends works that create **durable community assets** (such as roads, classrooms and drinking-water units) in their area. The money is **non-lapsable** — unspent funds are carried forward rather than returned — a fixed share is **earmarked for areas with SC and ST populations**, and **at least 10% of the sanctioned works** are inspected at the district level to check quality.

On the administrative side, the **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee** recommended a dedicated machinery for personnel management, and the **Department of Personnel** was created in **1970 under the Prime Minister** (following the First Administrative Reforms Commission of 1966). It is today the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT).

The **Deputy Speaker (Art 93/94)** is elected by the Lok Sabha from among its own members, presides when the Speaker's office is vacant, and can be removed by a resolution passed by an **effective majority** after 14 days' notice.

**Picture it**

| Topic | Key fact |
|---|---|
| MPLADS funds | Non-lapsable; carried forward |
| MPLADS purpose | Durable community assets; SC/ST earmark; 10% of works inspected |
| Department of Personnel | Created 1970, under the Prime Minister |
| Deputy Speaker | Art 93/94; elected by the House; removable by effective majority |

**Terms explained**
- **Non-lapsable** = money not spent in a year does not expire; it stays available in later years.
- **Durable community asset** = a lasting public work (not a one-off expense) that benefits the community.
- **Effective majority** = a majority of the members actually in office at the time (vacancies excluded).

**Don't confuse**
- MPLADS funds are **non-lapsable** — the common trap is to assume they lapse at the year's end.
- The Department of Personnel was placed under the **Prime Minister**, not the Home Ministry.

**Remember it**
"MPLADS money waits, it does not vanish" — unspent funds roll over.

**TL;DR**
- MPLADS: non-lapsable funds for durable community assets; a share earmarked for SC/ST areas; at least 10% of works inspected.
- The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 under the Prime Minister; the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee had urged it.
- Deputy Speaker (Art 93/94): elected by the Lok Sabha; removable by an effective-majority resolution.
keyPoints: MPLADS funds are non-lapsable, for durable community assets, with a share earmarked for SC/ST areas.
At least 10% of MPLADS works are inspected at the district level.
The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 under the PM; the N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee had urged reform.
The Deputy Speaker (Art 93/94) is elected by the Lok Sabha and removable by an effective-majority resolution.

items.title: The President in Full — Election, Impeachment, Vetoes, Ordinances & Pardons
items.body:
## The President, clause by clause

**In one line:** the President (Art 52) is the head of the Indian State, elected indirectly for five years, who acts on ministerial advice but holds a set of legal powers that exams test Article by Article.

**Why it is asked:** "Who is NOT in the electoral college?", "What majority impeaches the President?", "Which veto applies to a Money Bill?" and "Which case limited ordinances?" recur every year.

**The story**

### Election (Art 54, 55, 58, 71)
- **Electoral college (Art 54):** **elected** members of both Houses of Parliament + **elected** members of the State Legislative Assemblies + elected members of the Assemblies of **Delhi and Puducherry** (added by the **70th Amendment, 1992**).
- **Not in it:** **nominated** members of either House, **nominated** MLAs and members of **Legislative Councils**.
- **Value of votes (Art 55):** an MLA's vote = state population ÷ elected MLAs ÷ 1,000 (population of the **1971 census**); an MP's vote = total value of all MLAs' votes ÷ total elected MPs. This keeps **parity** between states and the Union.
- Method: **proportional representation by single transferable vote**, secret ballot.
- **Nomination:** at least **50 proposers and 50 seconders**; security deposit **₹15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India**.
- **Qualifications (Art 58):** citizen, **35 years**, qualified to be a **Lok Sabha** member, no office of profit. A sitting **Vice-President, Governor or Union/State minister** may contest (these are not offices of profit).
- **Disputes (Art 71):** decided by the **Supreme Court** only; acts done before the election is set aside stay valid.

### Office (Art 56-62)
- **Oath (Art 60):** before the **Chief Justice of India** (or the senior-most Supreme Court judge).
- **Conditions (Art 59):** not a member of any legislature; rent-free official residence; emoluments fixed by Parliament and **not reduced during the term**.
- **Immunity (Art 361):** no criminal proceedings during the term; civil proceedings only after **two months' notice**.
- **Resignation:** letter to the **Vice-President**.
- **Impeachment (Art 61):** only ground = **"violation of the Constitution"**; charges signed by **one-fourth** of the members of the House, **14 days' notice**; passed by **two-thirds of the total membership** of each House. **Nominated** members of Parliament **take part**; elected MLAs (who vote in the election) do **not**. No President has ever been impeached.
- **Vacancy (Art 62):** an election for a term ending must be held **before expiry**; a casual vacancy must be filled **within six months**. The new President gets a full five-year term. Meanwhile the **Vice-President** acts (Art 65); if both offices are vacant, the **Chief Justice of India** acts (President (Discharge of Functions) Act, **1969** — **M. Hidayatullah**, July–August 1969).

### Vetoes — what the President can do with each bill (Art 111)
| Bill | Assent | Absolute veto | Suspensive veto (return once) | Pocket veto |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ordinary bill | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Money Bill | Yes | Yes (withhold) | **No** — cannot return | No |
| Constitutional Amendment Bill | **Must** assent (**24th Amendment, 1971**) | No | No | No |
- **Absolute veto** used by **Rajendra Prasad (1954, PEPSU Appropriation Bill)** and **R. Venkataraman (1991, MPs' salary and pension amendment bill)**.
- **Pocket veto** — no time limit in the Constitution (unlike the US 10 days); used by **Zail Singh (1986, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill)**.
- Re-passed bill after a suspensive veto: the President **must** assent; re-passing needs only a **simple majority**.

### Ordinance (Art 123)
- Only when **either House is not in session**; must be laid before Parliament and lapses **six weeks after Parliament reassembles** — so the longest life is **six months and six weeks**.
- Can be retrospective; cannot amend the Constitution; can be withdrawn at any time.
- **R.C. Cooper (1970)**: satisfaction can be challenged for mala fides; the **38th Amendment (1975)** made it final; the **44th Amendment (1978)** removed that bar.
- **D.C. Wadhwa (1987)** and **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**: repeated **re-promulgation** is a **fraud on the Constitution**.

### Pardon (Art 72)
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Pardon** | Removes both sentence and conviction |
| **Commutation** | Lighter form of punishment (death → rigorous imprisonment) |
| **Remission** | Shorter period, same character |
| **Respite** | Lesser sentence for a special fact (pregnancy, disability) |
| **Reprieve** | **Stay** of execution, usually of a death sentence |
- Exercised **on ministerial advice** (**Maru Ram, 1980**); no right to an oral hearing (**Kehar Singh, 1989**); arbitrary use is reviewable (**Epuru Sudhakar, 2006** — Andhra Pradesh case).
- The Governor (Art 161) cannot pardon a **court-martial** sentence or **pardon** a death sentence.

### Other powers
- Appoints the **PM, ministers, AG, CAG, CEC and Election Commissioners, UPSC members, Governors, Finance Commission**; nominates **12** to the Rajya Sabha; is the **Supreme Commander** of the armed forces; addresses Parliament (Art 86-87); summons and prorogues the Houses and dissolves the Lok Sabha.
- **Discretion** (situational): choosing a PM in a **hung House** or when the PM dies without a successor; dismissing a ministry that has lost confidence; returning advice **once** (Art 74(1) proviso, **44th Amendment**).

### Presidents to remember
| President | Exam hook |
|---|---|
| Rajendra Prasad | First; only one with **two full terms** |
| Zakir Husain | First Muslim President; first to **die in office** (1969) |
| V.V. Giri | Acting President and later President |
| Neelam Sanjiva Reddy | Only President **elected unopposed** (1977); first Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh |
| K.R. Narayanan | First Dalit President |
| Pratibha Patil | First woman President |
| **Droupadi Murmu** | **15th** President since **25 July 2022**; first **tribal** woman |

## Don't confuse
- Election: **elected** MLAs vote, **nominated** MPs do not. Impeachment: **nominated** MPs vote, MLAs do not.
- President resigns to the **Vice-President**; Vice-President resigns to the **President**.

**TL;DR**
- Electoral college = elected MPs + elected MLAs (incl. Delhi, Puducherry); 50+50 nomination; ₹15,000 deposit.
- Impeachment: violation of the Constitution; 1/4 sign, 14 days; 2/3 of total membership of each House.
- Money Bill — no suspensive veto; Amendment Bill — assent compulsory (24th).
- Ordinance life: six months + six weeks; re-promulgation is a fraud (Krishna Kumar Singh 2017).
keyPoints: The Presidential electoral college excludes nominated MPs, nominated MLAs and Legislative Council members; Delhi and Puducherry MLAs were added by the 70th Amendment, 1992.
A presidential nomination needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders and a ₹15,000 deposit in the Reserve Bank of India.
Impeachment (Art 61): only for violation of the Constitution; 1/4 members sign, 14 days notice, two-thirds of the total membership of each House; nominated MPs take part.
The President cannot return a Money Bill and must assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill (24th Amendment, 1971); Zail Singh used the pocket veto in 1986.
An ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles; Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held repeated re-promulgation a fraud on the Constitution.
Pardon removes sentence and conviction; reprieve stays execution; respite lessens it for a special fact; Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allows judicial review.

items.title: Vice-President, PM, Council of Ministers & Attorney General in Full
items.body:
## The rest of the Union executive

**In one line:** the Vice-President is a standby head of state who chairs the Rajya Sabha; the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers hold real power; the Attorney General is the government's chief lawyer.

**Why it is asked:** election differences (President vs Vice-President), Articles 74-78 and 88, Cabinet vs Council and "who is in office now" are standard.

**The story**

### Vice-President (Art 63-71)
| Point | Rule |
|---|---|
| Electoral college (Art 66) | **All members** of both Houses — **elected and nominated**; **no MLAs** |
| Joint meeting | Not needed since the **11th Amendment (1961)** |
| Qualifications | Citizen, **35 years**, qualified for **Rajya Sabha** membership, no office of profit |
| Nomination | **20 proposers and 20 seconders**; ₹15,000 deposit |
| Oath (Art 69) | Before the **President** |
| Resignation | To the **President** |
| Removal (Art 67(b)) | Resolution **only in the Rajya Sabha**, **14 days' notice**, **effective majority**; agreed by the Lok Sabha by **simple majority**; **no ground** is stated |
| Acting President | Up to **six months**; then does **not** chair the Rajya Sabha and draws the **President's** salary |
| Salary | Paid as **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (no salary as Vice-President) |
| Article 70 | Parliament provides for the President's functions in other contingencies |
- Modelled on the **American** Vice-President, but the US one **succeeds** to the remaining term; India's only **acts** until a new election.
- **First:** S. Radhakrishnan. **Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned on **21 July 2025** on health grounds; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** won the early election of **9 September 2025** (452 votes against **B. Sudershan Reddy**'s 300) and became the **15th** Vice-President on **12 September 2025**.

### Prime Minister (Art 74, 75, 78)
- Appointed by the President (Art 75); convention: leader of the Lok Sabha majority. In a hung House the President uses **discretion** — first used in **1979** (**Charan Singh**).
- A non-member may be PM for **six months**; the PM may be from **either House** (Rajya Sabha PMs: **Indira Gandhi 1966, H.D. Deve Gowda 1996, I.K. Gujral 1997, Manmohan Singh 2004**).
- **Art 78** — duty of the PM to **communicate** all Cabinet decisions to the President and furnish information.
- Chairs **NITI Aayog**, the **Inter-State Council**, the **National Integration Council** and the **National Water Resources Council**; heads the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet.
- **Narendra Modi** — sworn in for a **third** consecutive term on **9 June 2024**; the first PM since Nehru to win three successive terms.
- PM's death or resignation **dissolves** the whole Council of Ministers.

### Council of Ministers (Art 74, 75, 77, 88)
- **Art 74(1):** aid and advice binding (**42nd Amendment, 1976**); President may send it back **once** (**44th, 1978**). **Art 74(2):** no court may inquire what advice was given.
- **Art 75(1A):** total ministers ≤ **15% of the Lok Sabha** (**91st Amendment, 2003**); **75(1B):** a member disqualified for **defection** cannot be a minister until re-elected.
- **Art 75(3):** collective responsibility to the **Lok Sabha**; **75(5):** a non-member minister gets **six months**.
- **No legal responsibility** — a minister need not **countersign** the President's orders (unlike Britain).
- **Art 77:** all executive action in the **President's name**; Business Rules.
- **Art 88:** ministers and the **Attorney General** may **speak** in either House, a joint sitting or a committee, but **vote** only where they are members.
- **Three tiers:** Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State (independent charge or attached), Deputy Ministers; **Parliamentary Secretaries** are outside it.
- **Cabinet** entered the Constitution only in **Art 352**, by the **44th Amendment (1978)**. A **Kitchen Cabinet** is the PM's informal inner circle — strong under **Indira Gandhi**.
- **Cabinet committees** (extra-constitutional): Political Affairs (the **"super cabinet"**), Economic Affairs, Appointments, Security, Parliamentary Affairs (advises on **summoning** Parliament); mostly headed by the PM.

### Attorney General (Art 76)
- Qualified to be a **Supreme Court judge**; appointed by the President; holds office **during the President's pleasure**; **no fixed term** and no retirement age in the Constitution.
- **Right of audience** in **all courts** of India; can speak in Parliament but **cannot vote** (Art 88); **not** a member of the Cabinet; may take **private practice** (not against the government).
- **First:** **M.C. Setalvad**. **Now: R. Venkataramani** (since 1 October 2022, reappointed 2025). The **Solicitor General** (**Tushar Mehta**) is a **statutory**, not constitutional, officer.

## Don't confuse
- President: elected MPs + elected MLAs; Vice-President: **all** MPs, **no** MLAs.
- President takes oath before the **CJI**; Vice-President before the **President**.
- AG — constitutional (Art 76); Solicitor General — statutory. Neither resigns automatically with the government in the Constitution.

**TL;DR**
- VP: all MPs elect; 20+20; removal begins only in the Rajya Sabha (effective majority).
- C.P. Radhakrishnan — 15th VP since 12 September 2025; PM Modi third term since 9 June 2024.
- Art 74 binding advice; Art 75 15% cap and defector bar; Art 78 PM informs President; Art 88 speak not vote.
- AG: SC-judge qualification, pleasure tenure, right of audience in all courts; R. Venkataramani.
keyPoints: The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses, elected and nominated, but no state MLAs; a nomination needs 20 proposers and 20 seconders.
The Vice-President takes oath before the President and resigns to the President; removal begins only in the Rajya Sabha with an effective majority, and no ground is required.
C.P. Radhakrishnan became the 15th Vice-President on 12 September 2025 after Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned on 21 July 2025.
Article 78 obliges the Prime Minister to communicate Cabinet decisions to the President; Article 77 says executive action is taken in the President's name.
The word Cabinet appears only in Article 352, inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978).

The Attorney General (Art 76) must be qualified as a Supreme Court judge, has a right of audience in all courts, and holds office during the pleasure of the President; R. Venkataramani holds the post.

items.title: Parliament in Full — Seats, Membership, Privileges & Money Bills
items.body:
## Who sits in Parliament and how a law is made

**In one line:** Parliament (Art 79) is the President plus two Houses whose seats, members' eligibility, privileges and bill rules are fixed in Articles 80-122.

**Why it is asked:** seat numbers, the women's reservation amendment, disqualification rules, Article 105 privileges and "which of these is a Money Bill" are regular statement questions.

**The story**

### Seats
| Item | Rajya Sabha (Art 80) | Lok Sabha (Art 81) |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum | **250** = 238 elected + **12 nominated** | 530 states + 20 UTs (+2 Anglo-Indians until 2020) |
| Now | **245** | **543** |
| Seat allocation | **Fourth Schedule**, by **population** (Uttar Pradesh most, **31**) | Territorial constituencies |
| Election | By elected MLAs, **STV**, **open ballot** (since 2003) | Direct, first-past-the-post |
- **Nominated (Art 80(3)):** persons with special knowledge of **literature, science, art and social service**.
- **UTs in the Rajya Sabha:** only **Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir**.
- **Andhra Pradesh** sends **25** members to the Lok Sabha and **11** to the Rajya Sabha.
- **Delimitation freeze:** state-wise seats fixed on the **1971 census** until the first census after **2026** (**42nd** and **84th Amendments**); boundaries were redrawn on the **2001** census (**87th Amendment, 2003**).
- **SC/ST seats:** **Art 330**. **Women: one-third** of seats (**106th Amendment, 2023** — *Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam*, **Art 330A**), effective after the next census and delimitation, for **15 years**.
- **Term (Art 83):** Lok Sabha **five years**; during a National Emergency Parliament may extend it **one year at a time**, but not beyond **six months** after the emergency ends. Rajya Sabha members serve **six years**, one-third retiring every two years.

### Membership
- **Qualifications (Art 84):** citizen; **oath** before a person authorised by the **Election Commission**; **30** years (Rajya Sabha), **25** (Lok Sabha). The RPA 1951 adds: be a registered **elector**. The **domicile** rule for Rajya Sabha was dropped in **2003** (upheld in **Kuldip Nayar, 2006**).
- **Disqualifications (Art 102):** office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged **insolvent**, not a citizen, or by law. **RPA:** conviction with **two years** or more of imprisonment. **Lily Thomas (2013)** struck down **Section 8(4)** (the 3-month appeal shield).
- **Who decides (Art 103):** the **President**, on the **Election Commission**'s opinion (binding). Defection questions go to the **presiding officer**.
- **Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985):** disqualification for **voluntarily giving up** party membership, **defying the whip**, an **independent** joining a party, or a **nominated** member joining a party **after six months**. A **merger** backed by **two-thirds** of the legislature party is exempt; the **91st Amendment (2003)** deleted the one-third **split** exception. **Kihoto Hollohan (1992)**: the Speaker's decision is open to **judicial review**; **Keisham Meghachandra (2020)**: decide within about **three months**.
- **Vacating seats (Art 101):** double membership, or **absence for 60 days** without permission.
- **Privileges (Art 105):** freedom of **speech** in the House, no court case for a vote or speech; freedom from **arrest in civil cases** 40 days before and after a session. **Sita Soren (2024)**: no immunity for **bribery**, overruling **P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**.
- **Art 99** oath (Third Schedule); **Art 100** quorum one-tenth; **Art 106** salaries by law; **Art 118** rules of procedure; **Art 120** Hindi or English; **Art 121** no discussion of a **judge's conduct** except on a removal motion; **Art 122** courts cannot question **proceedings**.

### Bills
| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| 107 | Ordinary bill: either House; does **not lapse on prorogation** |
| 109 | Money Bill procedure: **Lok Sabha only**, **President's recommendation**, Rajya Sabha **14 days** |
| 110 | Definition: **taxes, borrowing, Consolidated/Contingency Fund, appropriation, charged expenditure** |
| 117 | Financial Bills: **117(1)** like a Money Bill to introduce; **117(3)** recommendation needed only for **consideration** |
- **Not** Money Bills merely because they provide **fines**, **licence fees** or **local-authority taxes**.
- The **Speaker's certificate** is final (Art 110(3)); **K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar, 2018)** upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill; **Rojer Mathew (2019)** referred that question to a larger bench.

## Don't confuse
- **Art 102** (disqualification, President decides) vs **Tenth Schedule** (defection, Speaker/Chairman decides).
- **Art 117(1)** Financial Bill = Lok Sabha only; **117(3)** = either House.

**TL;DR**
- RS 250 (12 nominated), 245 now; LS 543 now; AP 25 LS + 11 RS.
- 106th Amendment 2023: one-third seats for women (Art 330A), after delimitation, for 15 years.
- Art 102 + RPA (2 years); Lily Thomas 2013; 10th Schedule 1985; Sita Soren 2024.
- Money Bill items: tax, borrowing, Consolidated Fund; fines and fees are not.
keyPoints: The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats by population; Uttar Pradesh has the most (31); only Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir among UTs are represented.
Andhra Pradesh has 25 Lok Sabha and 11 Rajya Sabha seats.
The 106th Amendment (2023), Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves one-third of Lok Sabha seats for women (Art 330A) for 15 years after delimitation.
Under Art 103 the President decides Art 102 disqualifications on the opinion of the Election Commission; Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4) of the RPA.
Sita Soren (2024) held that Article 105 gives no immunity for taking a bribe, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
A bill is not a Money Bill merely because it imposes fines or licence fees; K.S. Puttaswamy (2018) upheld the Aadhaar Act as a Money Bill.
Indian Parliament is modelled on the British Westminster (parliamentary) system.
The Representation of the People Act requires a candidate to be a registered elector in a parliamentary constituency.

items.title: Presiding Officers, Sessions & Parliamentary Devices in Full
items.body:
## Running the House

**In one line:** the Speaker and the Chairman run each House, sessions open and close by fixed rules, and members use a toolkit of questions and motions to hold the government to account.

**Why it is asked:** "To whom does the Speaker resign?", "Which bills lapse on dissolution?", "How many members support a no-confidence motion?" and closure types are routine traps.

**The story**

### Presiding officers
| Officer | Key rules |
|---|---|
| **Speaker** (Art 93-96) | Elected by the Lok Sabha; resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; removed by **effective majority** after **14 days' notice**; during a removal resolution cannot preside but may **speak and vote in the first instance** (no casting vote); does **not** vacate office on dissolution — stays until the new House **first meets** |
| **Deputy Speaker** | Resigns to the **Speaker**; post **vacant since 2019** (17th and 18th Lok Sabha) |
| **Speaker pro tem** | Appointed by the **President**, usually the senior-most member; swears in members (**Bhartruhari Mahtab, 2024**) |
| **Panel of Chairpersons** | Up to **10**, nominated by the Speaker; cannot preside when both Speaker and Deputy posts are vacant |
| **Chairman, Rajya Sabha** | The **Vice-President** (Art 64); does **not** certify Money Bills or preside at joint sittings |
| **Deputy Chairman** | **Harivansh Narayan Singh** (since 2018) |
- **Speaker Om Birla** (Kota) — re-elected on **26 June 2024** for the 18th Lok Sabha by **voice vote**; a motion for his **removal** was defeated by voice vote on **11 March 2026**. First Speaker: **G.V. Mavalankar**; first Deputy Speaker: **M. Ananthasayanam Ayyangar**.
- Speaker's salary is **charged** on the Consolidated Fund; ranks with the **CJI** (7th) in precedence; chairs the **Business Advisory**, **Rules** and **General Purposes** Committees and is ex-officio head of the **Indian Parliamentary Group**.
- **Leader of the Opposition:** leader of the largest opposition party with **one-tenth** of the seats; statutory since **1977**. Lok Sabha — **Rahul Gandhi** (since June 2024, the first recognised LoP since 2014); Rajya Sabha — **Mallikarjun Kharge**. Leader of the House: Lok Sabha — the **PM**; Rajya Sabha — **J.P. Nadda**.
- **Whip** — rests only on **convention**; not in the Constitution, the Rules or any statute.

### Sessions and lapse of bills
- **Art 85:** gap between sessions ≤ **six months**; summoned by the President on advice of the **Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs**. Sittings: **11 am–1 pm** and **2–6 pm**.
- **Adjournment sine die** — by the presiding officer, no date fixed. **Prorogation** — by the **President**; bills **do not lapse**.
- **Lapse on dissolution:** a bill **pending in the Lok Sabha** (even if from the Rajya Sabha) and a bill passed by the Lok Sabha **pending in the Rajya Sabha** lapse. **Do not lapse:** a bill pending in the Rajya Sabha and **not passed** by the Lok Sabha; a bill notified for a **joint sitting**; a bill awaiting **assent**; a bill **returned** by the President for reconsideration.
- **Quorum:** one-tenth (**55** in the Lok Sabha, **25** in the Rajya Sabha). **Lame-duck session:** the last session of an outgoing House.
- **Joint sitting order of presiding:** Speaker → Deputy Speaker → **Deputy Chairman** of the Rajya Sabha. **Official Languages Act 1963** kept English after 1965.
- **New Parliament building** inaugurated on **28 May 2023**.

### Devices
| Device | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Starred question** | **Oral** answer; supplementaries allowed (marked with an asterisk) |
| **Unstarred question** | **Written** answer; no supplementaries |
| **Short-notice question** | Less than **10 days'** notice; oral |
| **Zero Hour** | Indian innovation since **1962**; not in the rules |
| **Adjournment motion** | **Lok Sabha** only; **50** members; involves **censure**; debate of at least **2½ hours** |
| **Calling attention** | Indian innovation of **1954**; in the rules |
| **No-confidence motion** | **Rule 198**; **50** members; no reasons needed; whole ministry. First: **J.B. Kripalani** against **Nehru, 1963** |
| **Censure motion** | Must state **reasons**; may target a minister; passing it need not force resignation |
| **Short-duration discussion** | **Rule 193**; **two hours**; no formal motion |
| **Rule 377 / Special Mention** | Matter not covered elsewhere — Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha |
| **Closures** | **Simple**; **by compartments**; **kangaroo** (only important clauses debated); **guillotine** (undiscussed clauses voted) |
| **Motion of Thanks** | On the President's address; its defeat = defeat of the government |
- Confidence votes lost: **V.P. Singh (1990)**, **H.D. Deve Gowda (1997)**, **A.B. Vajpayee (1999, by one vote)**; **Morarji Desai** resigned in 1979 before a vote.
- **Resolutions:** private members' (alternate **Fridays**), government, statutory.

## Don't confuse
- Speaker resigns to the **Deputy Speaker**; Vice-President (Chairman) resigns to the **President**.
- **Adjournment** motion (censure, 50 members) vs **adjournment** of the House (presiding officer's order).

**TL;DR**
- Speaker: effective-majority removal, 14 days; stays in office after dissolution; Om Birla since 2019, re-elected 26 June 2024.
- LoP: one-tenth of seats; Rahul Gandhi (LS), Mallikarjun Kharge (RS).
- Bills awaiting assent or notified for a joint sitting survive dissolution.
- Adjournment and no-confidence motions need 50 members; Rule 193 short-duration discussion.
keyPoints: The Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker, is removed by an effective majority after 14 days notice, and continues in office after dissolution until the new House first meets.
The Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha has been vacant since 2019; Harivansh Narayan Singh is Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
Om Birla was re-elected Speaker on 26 June 2024; Rahul Gandhi is Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and Mallikarjun Kharge in the Rajya Sabha.
The Leader of the Opposition needs one-tenth of the seats and was given statutory recognition in 1977.
An adjournment motion is admitted only in the Lok Sabha with 50 members and involves censure; Rule 193 allows a two-hour short-duration discussion.
Kangaroo closure debates only important clauses; guillotine puts undiscussed clauses to vote.
Joint sittings have been held only three times — Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill (1978) and POTA Bill (2002).

items.title: Parliamentary Committees, the Budget Articles & MPLADS in Full
items.body:
## Money and scrutiny — the detail

**In one line:** committees do Parliament's detailed checking, a cluster of Articles (112-117, 265-267) governs public money, and MPLADS lets each MP steer local works.

**Why it is asked:** sizes and origins of committees, the difference between supplementary, additional and excess grants, and MPLADS rules are favourite one-liners.

**The story**

### Committees
| Committee | Members | Origin and features |
|---|---|---|
| **Public Accounts** | **22** (15 LS + 7 RS) | **1921** (GoI Act 1919); one-year term; chair from the **Opposition** since **1967**; **ministers cannot be members**; examines **CAG** reports |
| **Estimates** | **30**, **Lok Sabha only** | **1950**, on **John Mathai**'s advice; the **largest**; "continuous economy committee" |
| **Public Undertakings** | **22** (15 LS + 7 RS) | **1964**, **Krishna Menon** Committee |
| **Departmental Standing Committees** | **31** each (21 LS + 10 RS) | **1993** (17 at first); **24** since **2004** — **16** under the Lok Sabha and **8** under the Rajya Sabha |
| Petitions | 15 LS / 10 RS | Petitions on bills and public matters |
| Privileges | 15 LS / 10 RS | Breaches of privilege |
| Ethics | — | Rajya Sabha **1997**, Lok Sabha **2000** |
| Government Assurances | 15 LS / 10 RS | Ministers' promises |
| Subordinate Legislation | 15 LS | Delegated legislation |
| Welfare of SCs and STs | **30** (20 LS + 10 RS) | **1968** |
| Empowerment of Women | 30 | **1997** |
| Offices of Profit (Joint) | 15 (10 LS + 5 RS) | Which posts disqualify |
| Business Advisory | LS 15 | Chaired by the **Speaker**; time-table |
- **Ad hoc:** Select Committees (one House), **Joint Parliamentary Committees** (both Houses — Bofors 1987, Harshad Mehta securities scam 1992).
- **Consultative Committees** are run by the **Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs** and are **not** parliamentary committees.

### Budget Articles and funds
| Article | Rule |
|---|---|
| **112** | **Annual Financial Statement** — the word "budget" is not used |
| **113** | Charged expenditure **not votable** but discussable; demands only on the **President's recommendation** |
| **114** | **Appropriation Bill** — no amendment that varies the amount |
| **115** | **Supplementary**, **additional** and **excess** grants |
| **116** | **Vote on account**, **vote of credit**, **exceptional grant** |
| **117** | Financial Bills |
| **265** | No tax except by **authority of law** |
| **266** | **Consolidated Fund** and **Public Account** |
| **267** | **Contingency Fund** — at the **President's** disposal, held by the **Finance Secretary**; corpus **₹30,000 crore** |
- **Charged** items include the President's emoluments, salaries of the Speaker/Chairman and their deputies, Supreme Court judges' salaries, **High Court judges' pensions**, the **CAG**, **UPSC** expenses and **debt** charges.
- **Vote on account** — usually for **two months**, about one-sixth of the budget, until the Appropriation Act passes.
- **Excess grant** — voted only after the **PAC** approves it. **Token grant** — new service paid by **re-appropriation**.
- The **Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931** lets new taxes run before the Finance Bill passes; the Finance Bill must be enacted within **75 days**.
- **Budget date:** **1 February** since **2017** (earlier the last working day of February); the **Railway Budget** (separate since the **Acworth Committee, 1924**) merged in **2017**. First budget of independent India: **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty**, **26 November 1947**. **Nirmala Sitharaman** presented the **2026-27** budget in **February 2026** — her **ninth consecutive** budget, a record.

### MPLADS
- Launched on **23 December 1993**; run by the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation** since **October 1994**.
- **₹5 crore** per MP per year (since 2011-12); **suspended** in 2020-21 and 2021-22 for **COVID-19**.
- At least **15%** for areas inhabited by **SCs** and **7.5%** by **STs**.
- Lok Sabha MPs — their constituency; elected Rajya Sabha MPs — any district of their **state**; **nominated** MPs — **anywhere in India**.
- Works must create **durable community assets**.
- The **Department of Personnel** was set up in **1970** under the PM, after the **N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar** Committee and the first ARC (1966).
- Funds are **non-lapsable** and go to the **district authority**, which must inspect at least **10%** of works; up to **₹25 lakh** a year may be spent outside the state.

## Don't confuse
- **Additional grant** = new service not in the budget; **supplementary** = more money for an existing service; **excess** = spent more than granted.
- **PAC** looks at money spent; **Estimates** at money to be spent.

**TL;DR**
- PAC 22 (1921, opposition chair, no ministers); Estimates 30 LS (1950, largest); PUC 22 (1964); 24 DRSCs of 31.
- Art 112 AFS, 113 charged, 114 appropriation, 115 extra grants, 116 vote on account, 266-267 funds.
- MPLADS: ₹5 crore, 15% SC / 7.5% ST, non-lapsable, 10% inspected, nominated MPs anywhere.
keyPoints: The chairman of the Public Accounts Committee has come from the Opposition since 1967, and ministers cannot be members.
There are 24 Departmental Standing Committees of 31 members each — 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.
Article 115 covers supplementary, additional and excess grants; Article 116 covers vote on account, vote of credit and exceptional grants.
The Contingency Fund of India (Art 267) is at the disposal of the President, held by the Finance Secretary, with a corpus of ₹30,000 crore.
The budget has been presented on 1 February since 2017, when the Railway Budget was merged; Nirmala Sitharaman presented the 2026-27 budget in February 2026, her ninth consecutive budget.
MPLADS: ₹5 crore per MP per year, 15% for SC and 7.5% for ST areas, non-lapsable funds, nominated MPs may choose works anywhere in India.
Cut motions: a Policy Cut reduces a demand to Re 1; an Economy Cut by a specified amount; a Token Cut by ₹100.

items.title: For Mains — Union Executive & Parliament
items.body:
### For Mains — Union Executive and Parliament

**In one line**
Mains questions on the Union executive and Parliament rarely ask "what" — they ask whether these institutions still deliver accountable, deliberative government, and what reforms would help.

**Why it is asked (Mains clauses M3-1 and M3-4)**
Paper-3 lists "Constitution and salient features; Union and State functions and duties" (M3-1) and "Parliament and State Legislatures — structure, powers, privileges" (M3-4). Expect analytical 10/15-mark questions, not fact recall.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Features | Parliamentary (Westminster) model; nominal versus real executive; bicameralism |
| Significance | Legislative scrutiny, executive accountability, the Rajya Sabha's federal voice |
| Problems | Falling sitting days, fewer bills to committees, disruptions, ordinance over-use, the Money-Bill route to bypass the Rajya Sabha |
| Reforms | More committee referral, a fixed calendar, anti-defection review, productivity norms |

**Data and authorities to quote**
- PRS Legislative Research: Parliament's sitting days have fallen sharply since the 1950s, and a shrinking share of bills is referred to committees.
- 2nd Administrative Reforms Commission (2005-09) and the NCRWC (2002): strengthen committees and limit ordinances.
- Judgments: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017) held that re-promulgating ordinances is a "fraud on the Constitution"; Kihoto Hollohan (1992) made the Speaker's anti-defection decisions open to judicial review; Rojer Mathew (2019) reopened the Money-Bill-route debate.
- 91st Amendment (2003): the 15% cap on the Council of Ministers.

**The AP angle**
Andhra Pradesh's Rajya Sabha members are its channel to press special-category-status and Krishna-Godavari river-water concerns in Union law-making — a concrete illustration of the Rajya Sabha as a federal chamber.

**Use in answers**
- Example: cite falling sitting days and low committee referral to argue that scrutiny is weakening.
- Quote: B. R. Ambedkar valued "responsibility" over "stability" in the parliamentary system.
- Diagram idea: a bill's journey (introduction, committee, both Houses, President), marking where scrutiny leaks.

**TL;DR**
- Frame answers around accountability and deliberation, not definitions.
- Quote PRS data, the 2nd ARC, and Krishna Kumar Singh (2017).
- Always add the Rajya-Sabha-as-federal-voice point with an AP example.
keyPoints: Mains clauses M3-1 and M3-4 test accountability and reform, not recall of facts.
Use the dimensions table: features, significance, problems, reforms.
Quote PRS sitting-day data, the 2nd ARC, the 91st Amendment and Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017).
AP angle: the Rajya Sabha as the state's federal voice on special status and river-water disputes.
